3. Compositional analysis

Source: vignettes/compositional_analysis.Rmd
compositional_analysis.Rmd

Continue in the same session. This block fits a donor-level model of immune cell-type proportions with sccomp (Mangiola et al. 2023).

library(dplyr)
library(cellNexusWorkshop)
library(sccomp)

if (!exists("obs_lung")) {
  library(cellNexus)
  dataset_ids <- respiratory_dataset_ids()
  cell_types_query <- c(immune_cell_types(), epithelial_cell_types())
  obs_lung <- get_metadata() |>
    keep_quality_cells() |>
    dplyr::filter(
      dataset_id %in% dataset_ids,
      cell_type_unified_ensemble %in% cell_types_query,
      age_days >= 365,
      age_days < 80 * 365
    ) |>
    join_census_tissue() |>
    annotate_cell_nexus(min_cells_per_sample = 50)
}

Why a composition model

A proportion vector sums to one, so an increase in one cell type forces a decrease somewhere else. Counts are overdispersed relative to a binomial. One dissociated sample can move an entire effect. sccomp models the sample composition jointly, estimates a mean-variability association, and has an explicit outlier pass.

The denominator is the immune compartment. Epithelial recovery depends on how hard the tissue was digested. A study that recovered many pneumocytes would push every immune proportion down, and that shift would enter the model as if it were age. Epithelial cells stay in obs_lung for the expression article.

obs_composition <- obs_lung |>
  dplyr::filter(cell_type_unified_ensemble %in% immune_cell_types()) |>
  # sccomp stores covariates in one column. A logical cannot share that
  # column with a character study id. "FALSE" is the reference level.
  dplyr::mutate(age_binary = as.character(age_binary))

obs_composition |>
  dplyr::count(cell_type_unified_ensemble, name = "n_cells") |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(n_cells))

Fit

The formula is ~ age_binary + dataset_id. sample_id is the replicate. cell_type_unified_ensemble is the group. dataset_id is a fixed effect, so the age contrast is within study. That is why Exercise 3 matters: a study with one age class competes with the age term.

bimodal_mean_variability_association = TRUE lets rare and abundant cell types follow different variability regimes.

The session default is pathfinder, which is fast enough to finish in the room. A result you would report uses Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (inference_method = "hmc"). Pathfinder intervals are a working approximation. Refit with "hmc" before you quote an effect, and read the sampler diagnostics on that fit. Set CELLNEXUS_WORKSHOP_INFERENCE=hmc for that fit. The first call compiles the Stan model and can take several minutes on top of the fit.

inference_method <- Sys.getenv("CELLNEXUS_WORKSHOP_INFERENCE", "pathfinder")

sccomp_res <- obs_composition |>
  sccomp_estimate(
    formula_composition = ~ age_binary + dataset_id,
    sample = "sample_id",
    cell_group = "cell_type_unified_ensemble",
    bimodal_mean_variability_association = TRUE,
    inference_method = inference_method
  ) |>
  sccomp_remove_outliers() |>
  sccomp_test()

Outlier removal refits the model with aberrant samples down-weighted. Removal comes before the test, because the test reads the refitted model. Look at which samples were flagged before accepting the correction. A flag concentrated in one study is a finding of its own.

sccomp_res |>
  dplyr::filter(factor == "age_binary") |>
  dplyr::select(cell_type_unified_ensemble, dplyr::starts_with("c_"), c_FDR)
## sccomp model
## ============
## 
## Model specifications:
##   Family: multi_beta_binomial 
##   Composition formula: ~age_binary + dataset_id 
##   Variability formula: ~1 
##   Inference method: pathfinder 
## 
## Data: Samples: 327   Cell groups: 26 
## 
## Column prefixes: c_ -> composition parameters  v_ -> variability parameters
## 
## Convergence diagnostics:
##   For each parameter, n_eff is the effective sample size and R_k_hat is the potential
##   scale reduction factor on split chains (at convergence, R_k_hat = 1).
## 
## # A tibble: 26 x 9
##    cell_type_unified_ensemble  c_lower c_effect c_upper  c_pH0   c_FDR c_rhat
##    <chr>                         <dbl>    <dbl>   <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>  <dbl>
##  1 b memory                   -0.104    0.123    0.344  0.418  0.162    1.000

##  3 cd14 mono                   0.144    0.354    0.568  0.0110 0.00285  1.00 
##  4 cd16 mono                  -0.297   -0.0458   0.194  0.669  0.26     1.000
##  5 cd4 fh em                  -0.320   -0.0201   0.276  0.705  0.279    1.00 
##  6 cd4 naive                  -0.148    0.0706   0.287  0.612  0.241    1.000
##  7 cd4 tcm                     0.138    0.362    0.585  0.0130 0.00454  1.000
##  8 cd4 tem                     0.376    0.622    0.872  0      0        1.00 
##  9 cd4 th1 em                 -0.258    0.00182  0.255  0.789  0.319    1.000
## 10 cd4 th1/th17 em            -0.00574  0.215    0.432  0.148  0.0528   1.00 
## # i 16 more rows
## # i 2 more variables: c_ess_bulk <dbl>, c_ess_tail <dbl>

Columns whose names start with c_ carry the age effect, its interval, c_FDR, and sampler diagnostics. On an HMC fit, c_rhat near 1 and a large effective sample size are the checks you want. The effect is on the model’s composition scale. Exponentiating it as a fold change in proportion is the wrong transformation. Say “the proportion of this cell type”.

An effect is a change in share. Because shares sum to one, one real change produces mirror-image changes in other labels. The label set is part of the result: this fit is a shift inside the immune compartment.

Plot

age_binary has two levels, so the summary is a boxplot. remove_unwanted_effects = TRUE shows proportions after the study term has been regressed out, which is the visual counterpart of the model. The blue box is the posterior predictive check (Gabry et al. 2019): the distribution of data the model would produce. Overlap between the observed points and that distribution is evidence that the model describes these data.

sccomp_boxplot(
  sccomp_res,
  factor = "age_binary",
  significance_threshold = 0.05,
  remove_unwanted_effects = TRUE
)

Exercise 6. Which cell types have c_FDR < 0.05 for factor == "age_binary"? For each, is the estimated effect higher or lower in donors over 50?

Solution 
sccomp_res |>
  dplyr::filter(factor == "age_binary", c_FDR < 0.05) |>
  dplyr::select(cell_type_unified_ensemble, dplyr::starts_with("c_"), c_FDR)

Read the sign of the effect column together with the boxplot. The contrast is donors over 50 against the reference level "FALSE" (50 and under), because age_binary was stored as character with "FALSE" first.

Exercise 7. Write one sentence on why epithelial, pneumocyte, and secretory are absent from this fit. What question would the model answer if they were added back?

Solution

Epithelial, pneumocyte, and secretory labels are left out so the proportions are shares of the immune compartment. Dissociation efficiency changes epithelial yield from study to study, and that technical shift would move every immune proportion. Adding the epithelial labels back answers a different question: change in share among immune and epithelial cells together. Report the label set with the effects.

If the fit is too slow for the time left, refit on a shorter label list (for example macrophage, CD14 monocytes, NK, naive and effector-memory T cells, naive B cells) and say so. The denominator changes, so the effects are a different question.
